name: Artic Rose
approach: Take US-2 east from Seattle/Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway (now Tye Rd), which heads toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite; park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn roughly 1.4 miles from US-2. From there, the on-foot approach follows only faint boot-path traces through open old-growth forest, generally trending uphill and left across a drainage to reach the base of the crag. Expect about 1,000 feet of elevation gain and 45-60 minutes of hiking, with route-finding skills helpful since the tread is intermittent.
descent: Single 85-foot rappel from fixed anchors.
itinerary: Casual day trip: 0.5 hour drive, 1.25 hour approach, 1 hour climbing, 0.5 hour descent.

approach: Take US-2 east from Seattle/Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway (now Tye Rd), which heads toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite; park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn roughly 1.4 miles from US-2. name: Blood Sport
approach: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area and park at the Alpental ski-area lot (the Snow Lake trailhead parking) or in a legal spot along Alpental Road itself. The side roads named 'Strasse' are private, and since 2021 residents have barred climbers from driving or walking on them. For the south-face/rock routes, the crag rises directly above the parking area with essentially no approach hike required. For routes on other aspects of the mountain, use the Commonwealth Basin/PCT North Trailhead a short distance up the highway instead, following the Pacific Crest Trail into Commonwealth Basin before cutting up toward the peak. Because of the short, direct access, Guye Peak is climbed both summer and winter, though rock routes are primarily a snow-free-season (summer-fall) objective.
descent: Lower off the 2-bolt chain anchor.
itinerary: An hour or two, and best treated as an add-on rather than a destination. Drive from Seattle in about 45 minutes, walk in through the boulder field and alder, warm up, work the route, and go. It pairs naturally with the South Rib if you want to make a day of Guye's south side, or with the rest of the Snoqualmie Pass area sport crags.

waypoints.name: Alpental Ski Area / Snow Lake Trailhead parking lot

name: Bowling Alley (aka Regular Route)
approach: From the NF-77 pullout, a well-used trail runs along the base of the formation. The West Face and North Side are different aspects of the same rock reached via short spurs off this main trail, generally under 15 minutes' walk from the parking pullout.
descent: Rappel from the anchor near a tree at the north end of the formation (2 raps with a 60m rope, or 1 rap with 2 ropes)
itinerary: Single-day outing: drive the forest roads to the NF-77 pullout, rack up and walk in (a few minutes) to the base, climb the 4-pitch route, rappel back to the base, and hike out to the car — easily done in half a day.

name: Cobbles 101
approach: From the NF-77 pullout, a well-used trail runs along the base of the formation. The West Face and North Side are different aspects of the same rock reached via short spurs off this main trail, generally under 15 minutes' walk from the parking pullout.
descent: Rappel from the anchor near a tree at the north end of the formation (2 raps with a 60m rope, or 1 rap with 2 ropes)
itinerary: Single-day outing: drive the forest roads to the NF-77 pullout, rack up and walk in (a few minutes) to the base, climb the 5-pitch route, rappel back to the base, and hike out to the car — easily done in half a day.

name: Deep Blue
approach: Identical to Vanishing Point's approach from the Barclay Lake Trailhead (see that route) — Barclay Creek Trail to the wash/gully system, fixed-line forested rib, and roped approach slabs to the base of the tower; Deep Blue's start is about 100 ft left of Vanishing Point's first pitch.
descent: Walk off the back of the tower (about 2.5-3 hours to the main climbers' trail), or rappel the route on its bolted anchors with a 70 m rope.
itinerary: A long single day for a strong party, or a two-day outing with a bivy at the base of the tower after approaching the evening before. Multiple parties have completed the route in a day without simuling, so linking pitches is an option rather than a requirement. Given the 5.13c crux, most parties working the route treat it as a multi-visit project rather than an onsight day out.

waypoints.name: Dolomite Tower (area pin / route top-out vicinity)

name: The Dirty
approach: From Naches, take US-12 west roughly 23 miles to just past the Rimrock Lake Dam, then turn south onto Tieton Reservoir Road (FR-1200). For the popular rock routes on the eastern cliffs, park in one of the pullouts along Tieton Road near a spring marked by a split-rail fence and follow the steep climbers' trail uphill to the base of the routes. To reach the summit via the non-technical Southwest Ridge, continue on FR-1200 to the South Fork/campground turnoff, park near the restroom area, and hike cross-country, following criss-crossing boot-paths while staying on the ridge crest until it becomes an established path to the summit block. The area melts out quickly and is climbable from May through November.
descent: Rappel via rocky gully with one rappel midway down, or descend via the Gangsta Rap route. Multiple rappels or rappel-to-rappel descent with one midway rappel.
itinerary: Single long day: drive to the Tieton Road pullout, approach ~20-40 minutes via the spring trail and traverse, climb 7 roped pitches (about 5 hours of climbing for one party), then descend via rappel or the gully walk-off. Parties report roughly 8-8.5 hours car-to-car at an unhurried pace.

waypoints.name: Tieton Reservoir Road (FR 1200) pullout, ~2.1 mi south of US-12, near the spring

name: Ephemeral
approach: From the large pullout at the SR-20 hairpin turn east of Washington Pass, follow the climbers' path uphill toward Spire Gully and the Quicksilver Slabs, then cut right into the dry creek bed below the chasm. Cross left beneath the first slab and scramble 3rd-class ground up the left edge of the smooth, slippery slabs into the Ice Box (a fixed line has been in place on the entry slab). Allow about 15 minutes from the car; expect snow on the approach early in the season.
descent: Lower off the bolted anchors.
itinerary: A short afternoon outing: drive to the hairpin pullout, make the 15-minute scramble approach into the Ice Box, climb the route, then lower and walk back to the car.

waypoints.name: Hairpin Turn pullout (Hwy 20 roadside parking, Washington Pass)
Ice Box right side / Ephemeral base
Ice Box (right side) formation, Hairpin Crags

name: EZ Way
approach: From Randle, drive south on Forest Road 25 to Forest Road 2551, just south of Elk Pass, then east on FR2551 for about 1.6 miles to an unmarked spur on the left; park at or just past the spur. From the parking spur, short flagged connector paths lead to the Boundary Trail. Follow the Boundary Trail 2.25 miles to Badger Lake, then continue 2.75 miles and about 700 feet of elevation gain to the last switchback below the ridge crest; from there an almost-level traverse through open timber breaks out onto the open west face of Shark Rock.
descent: Rappel or downclimb the route; descend back via the west slope to Boundary Trail junction.
itinerary: Single long day: early/pre-dawn start from the trailhead; hike about five miles on the Boundary Trail past Badger Lake, then a short traverse off the trail to the base of Shark Rock's west face (most of the morning); climb EZ Way (one pitch plus scrambling); rappel and reverse the approach for the long hike out, aiming to be off the ridge before dark given the remoteness.

name: Glacier View Temple
approach: From Seattle, drive east on I-90 to Snoqualmie Pass and take Exit 54, crossing to the north side of the freeway before turning onto FR 4832, then following it onto FR 4934 to the small trailhead pullout. On foot, cross the road and hike up a spur road for about 15 minutes to a flat bench, then pick up a cairned trail heading north into the forest to a rocky area, staying on the main climber's trail through a short, steeper forest section to reach the crag — roughly 25-30 minutes total from the car. A Northwest Forest Pass is generally expected for parking at national forest trailheads in this corridor.
descent: Lower off the chain anchor with a single rope.
itinerary: Single crag day: drive FR-4832/4934 to the parking area (~45-60 min from I-90), hike ~15-25 min to the East Face staging area, climb Glacier View Temple and other East Face sport lines, lower off each route, hike back out to the car.

waypoints.name: East Face wall top-out, Keechelus Ridge

name: Half Fast
approach: Take US-2 east from Seattle/Everett over Stevens Pass, then drop onto the old Stevens Pass Highway (now Tye Rd), which heads toward the Iron Horse Trailhead and the Wellington townsite; park in the pullout just uphill of a double hairpin turn roughly 1.4 miles from US-2. From there, the on-foot approach follows only faint boot-path traces through open old-growth forest, generally trending uphill and left across a drainage to reach the base of the crag. Expect about 1,000 feet of elevation gain and 45-60 minutes of hiking, with route-finding skills helpful since the tread is intermittent.
descent: Single rappel down fixed anchors.
itinerary: Day trip with driving and approach totaling 3-4 hours round trip.

waypoints.name: Tye Road / Old Stevens Pass Highway pullout (near double hairpin turn, ~1.4 mi from US 2)

name: Iceman
approach: Park at the apex of the hairpin turn on SR-20 below Washington Pass. Follow the climbers' trail up toward Quicksilver Slab and Spire Gully, then cut right into a dry creek bed and climb the slabs above it into the Ice Box. The upper, entrance slab has a fixed line; the lower slab does not. Both are smooth and slippery, and worse when wet.
descent: Lower or rappel from the anchor back to the base.
itinerary: A single-day cragging objective, typically combined with Route C and/or Route D at the same crag: drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20, approach via the slab/creek-bed trail, climb, then lower/rappel and retrace the approach to the car.

name: Junior's Farm
approach: From the parking pullout on spur 270, an unmarked climbers' path ascends directly up the boulder field on the hillside toward Tyler Peak Crags; there is no formal trailhead sign. The Full Montey sits on the upper bench of the Tyler Peak crag system, reached by climbing up past the base of the adjacent Mossness wall/sector to gain the upper bench. Because the approach trail is unofficial and unsigned, most parties rely on a written area description or GPS beta rather than a marked trail; expect a steep, brushy bushwhack-and-boulder-hop of a few hundred vertical feet from the road.
descent: Rappel descent from grassy ledge area above pitch 8 via multiple anchors. A single 60 m rope reaches the ground only if you use every anchor station—do not skip or link stations low on the descent.
itinerary: Single long day: ~5-minute approach from the car up the boulder field to the base of Mossness Wall, climb the 8 roped pitches (5.5-5.9) plus 2 scramble sections to the upper bench of Full Montey, then rappel back down to the boulder field (partway down, the rappel route leaves the climbing line for a gully to climber's right) and walk out. Plan for 6+ hours car-to-car.

waypoints.name: The Full Montey / Junior's Farm base area

name: Lone Wolf
approach: From I-90 Exit 54 (Hyak), follow Hyak Drive onto Forest Service Road NF-9070, continuing past where the pavement ends to the junction at Ollallie Meadow where the Pacific Crest Trail crosses the road. Take the left fork of NF-9070 and follow it until the road terminates in a large turnaround just below Silver Basin. From that turnaround, it's roughly a 20-30 minute approach on foot up into Silver Basin to reach the base of The Citadel's walls, including Sofa King Buttress on the NW side of the basin's east wall. The road is not plowed and is generally only clear of snow from around July through November.
descent: Rappel the route from bolted chain anchors atop each pitch.
itinerary: A half-day, single-pitch-crag-style outing: drive to the FR-9070 turnaround, hike ~20-30 minutes into Silver Basin to the base of The Obelisk, climb the 2-pitch Lone Wolf, rappel via the chain anchors, and hike back out to the car.

waypoints.name: FR-9070 / PCT (#2000) junction near Olallie Meadow, Snoqualmie Pass

name: Tepeh Towers
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From the basin, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) up the Eldorado Glacier to the high camp near 7,600 ft where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. From the Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp (~7,600 ft), rope up and walk about 45 minutes north-northwest across the glacier to where the towers rise out of the icecap, on the arête that divides the Inspiration Glacier from the McAllister Glacier.

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A bear canister is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

itinerary: Day 1: approach to Eldorado high camp (~7,600 ft) via Eldorado Creek and Eldorado Glacier. Day 2: ~45 min glacier approach north/northwest to Tepeh Towers, climb the short route (~30 min), return to camp or continue on to Austera Peak. Day 3: hike out.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek / Cascade River Road TH

name: North Face of The Mole
descent: A three-rappel descent heads east, ending near a prominent chockstone chimney. Rappel stations are single-anchor with additional cordage. Alternative: scramble down the gully.
itinerary: Day 1: Drive to Hook Creek Boulder parking area, hike to Edward Mesa or alpine camp (5,000+ ft elevation gain, 6-8 hours). Day 2: Approach The Mole base (40 minutes), climb North Face (3-4 hours), descend. Day 3: Descend to vehicles (2-3 hours).

waypoints.name: Icicle Creek Road roadside parking (Hook Creek Drainage)
Hook Creek Drainage / Mole approach area
The Mole (Edward Peak) North Face topout

name: On the Prowl (D)
approach: Park at the hairpin switchback on SR-20 between the Washington Pass summit and Early Winters/Mazama. Follow the climbers' trail up toward the chasm/gully right of the drainage, cross left below a slab, then scramble 3rd-class terrain up the left margin of the slabs into the Ice Box — about 15 minutes from the car. This route starts at the downhill (right-hand, toward-the-hairpin) end of the wall.
descent: Lower from the bolted, hook-equipped anchor at the top.
itinerary: A short afternoon outing: drive to the hairpin pullout, make the 15-minute scramble approach into the Ice Box, climb the route, then lower and walk back to the car.

waypoints.name: Ice Box right side (base of wall)

name: Particulate Matter
approach: From the large pullout at the SR-20 hairpin turn east of Washington Pass, follow the climbers' path uphill toward Spire Gully and the Quicksilver Slabs, then cut right into the dry creek bed below the chasm. Cross left beneath the first slab and scramble 3rd-class ground up the left edge of the smooth, slippery slabs into the Ice Box (a fixed line has been in place on the entry slab). Allow about 15 minutes from the car; expect snow on the approach early in the season.
descent: Lower off the bolted anchors.
itinerary: A short afternoon outing: drive to the hairpin pullout, make the 15-minute scramble approach into the Ice Box, climb one or more of the short bolted lines, then lower and walk back to the car — no camping or multi-day logistics required.

waypoints.name: SR-20 Hairpin pullout (Kangaroo Temple / Spire Gully)

name: Project Crack
approach: From Seattle, drive east on I-90 to Snoqualmie Pass and take Exit 54, crossing to the north side of the freeway before turning onto FR 4832, then following it onto FR 4934 to the small trailhead pullout. On foot, cross the road and hike up a spur road for about 15 minutes to a flat bench, then pick up a cairned trail heading north into the forest to a rocky area, staying on the main climber's trail through a short, steeper forest section to reach the crag — roughly 25-30 minutes total from the car. A Northwest Forest Pass is generally expected for parking at national forest trailheads in this corridor.
descent: Lower off the chain anchor with a single rope.
itinerary: Single crag day: drive FR-4832/4934 to the parking area, hike ~15-25 min to the East Face staging area, walk the talus base around to the route, lead the crack, lower off, return via the same approach trail.

waypoints.name: East Face wall top-out, Keechelus Ridge

name: Ride the Lightning
approach: From Naches, take US-12 west roughly 23 miles to just past the Rimrock Lake Dam, then turn south onto Tieton Reservoir Road (FR-1200). For the popular rock routes on the eastern cliffs, park in one of the pullouts along Tieton Road near a spring marked by a split-rail fence and follow the steep climbers' trail uphill to the base of the routes. To reach the summit via the non-technical Southwest Ridge, continue on FR-1200 to the South Fork/campground turnoff, park near the restroom area, and hike cross-country, following criss-crossing boot-paths while staying on the ridge crest until it becomes an established path to the summit block. The area melts out quickly and is climbable from May through November.
descent: Walk off climber's left via an obvious gully with one rappel required midway. A party that stops at or below the top of pitch 5 can instead rappel the bolted belays, with two ropes.
itinerary: Single long day: drive to the Tieton Road pullout, approach ~15 minutes on foot, climb 6-7 pitches (roughly 5.5-6 hours climbing per one detailed TR, 9am-6:30pm total), then rappel or walk off. Total car-to-car time of about 9.5 hours has been reported.

waypoints.name: Tieton Reservoir Road (FR 1200) pullout, ~2.1 mi south of US-12, near the spring

name: Roofer Madness
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
descent: Rappel or lower off the route's bolted anchors.
itinerary: Usually climbed as a short add-on before/after approaching to Roan Wall, or while based at the Martha's Place bivy, rather than as a standalone full-day objective.

name: Route C
approach: Spire Gully right (Alpenkuhl), part of the Hairpin Crags, is reached from the same large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 near Washington Pass used for Kangaroo Temple. Looking up toward South Early Winter Spire from the pullout, Spire Gully is the obvious gully just below and left; Alpenkuhl is its sunnier, south-facing right side (the left side is known as Tiger Wall). The approach is one of the shortest at Washington Pass — a direct walk/scramble of roughly 10-15 minutes straight up from the highway, snow-covered in early season and a worn boot path later in summer.
descent: Lower off the chain anchors.
itinerary: A single-day cragging objective, commonly linked with Route D and/or Iceman at the same crag: drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20, approach via the slab/creek-bed trail, climb, then lower off and retrace the approach to the car.

name: Route D
approach: Spire Gully right (Alpenkuhl), part of the Hairpin Crags, is reached from the same large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 near Washington Pass used for Kangaroo Temple. Looking up toward South Early Winter Spire from the pullout, Spire Gully is the obvious gully just below and left; Alpenkuhl is its sunnier, south-facing right side (the left side is known as Tiger Wall). The approach is one of the shortest at Washington Pass — a direct walk/scramble of roughly 10-15 minutes straight up from the highway, snow-covered in early season and a worn boot path later in summer.
descent: Lower off the chain anchors.
itinerary: A single-day cragging objective, commonly linked with Route C and/or Iceman at the same crag: drive to the hairpin turn on SR-20, approach via the slab/creek-bed trail, climb, then lower off and retrace the approach to the car.

name: Smears, Jugs, and Rock & Roll
descent: Downclimb or rappel from the anchors/boulder at the top (typically short rappel to ground level given the 30 ft length).
itinerary: Day 1: Hike from Snow Lakes Trailhead to Lake Viviane (6-8 hours with full pack). Establish camp at Viviane Campsite. Day 2: Acclimatization day; scout the route and set up top-rope if desired. Day 3: Climb Smears, Jugs, and Rock & Roll (1-2 hours of climbing). Day 4: Descent to trailhead (5-6 hours).

waypoints.name: Base of Prusik Peak south face (approximate)

name: Wild Wild West
approach: From Randle, WA (Hwy 12), head south on Hwy 131, keep right and follow NF-25 for 19.2 miles. After milepost 21, turn left at the sign for Mosquito Meadows onto NF-28 and follow it for 2.7 miles, then turn left onto NF-77. Continue on this rough, high-clearance-recommended road for about 2 miles until Pinto Rock comes into view, then continue to the large pullout where the main climber's trail is clearly visible. (Alternative approach from the Portland area: I-5 north to Woodland, WA; take Exit 21 and drive WA-503 east 32.5 miles toward NF-25.) From the pullout, walk up the road toward the wall to reach the base of the West Face, or hike around via the East Face, through the gap, and drop down to the left.
descent: Rappel from the summit.
itinerary: Single-day outing: drive to the NF-77 pullout, approach directly to the wall base (short walk), climb 4 pitches (Grade II, a few hours round trip for a competent team), then rappel off the north end of the formation.
